questions.question_text:
A fair six-sided die is rolled $45$ times and $X$ is the number of rolls that show an odd number.
Is $X$ a binomial random variable?

options.text: Yes — there are $45$ fixed trials, each roll is odd or it is not, the rolls are independent, and $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ every time.
Yes — but only because $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$, since a binomial variable needs equally likely outcomes.
options.why: Treats $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$ as a condition; a binomial variable allows any fixed $p$ between $0$ and $1$.

options.text: No — each roll has six possible outcomes, so a trial does not have exactly two outcomes.
options.why: Counts the faces of the die instead of the two recorded outcomes, odd or not odd.

options.text: No — the $45$ rolls all use the same die, so they cannot be independent of one another.
options.why: Assumes reusing one die creates dependence, but separate rolls do not affect each other.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the roll shows an odd number.
$n=45$ is fixed, each roll is odd or not odd, the rolls do not affect one another, and $p=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}$ every time.
All four conditions hold, so $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(45,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is binomial.

questions.question_text:
Nine cards are dealt one at a time, without replacement, from a shuffled standard deck, and $X$ is the number of spades among them.
Is $X$ a binomial random variable?

options.text: No — the trials are not independent, because $p$ changes as cards are removed and not replaced.
No — the number of trials is not fixed.
options.why: Nine cards are dealt, so $n=9$ is fixed; it is the independence condition that fails.

options.text: Yes — there are $9$ fixed trials and each card is a spade or it is not.
options.why: Checks only fixed $n$ and two outcomes, ignoring that $p$ changes when cards are not replaced.

options.text: Yes — the deck is shuffled, so every card dealt is equally likely to be a spade.
options.why: Shuffling makes a single draw fair but does not stop earlier cards from changing the chances for later ones.

questions.solution_text:
Success: a card dealt is a spade.
The first card is a spade with probability $\dfrac{13}{52}$, but after a spade is dealt the next card is a spade with probability $\dfrac{12}{51}$.
Because the cards are not replaced, the trials are not independent and $p$ is not constant, so $X$ is not binomial.

questions.question_text:
A biased coin shows a head with probability $0.7$.
It is tossed $16$ times, independently, and $X$ is the number of heads.
Which distribution describes $X$?

options.why: Used the probability of a tail, which is the failure probability, as $p$.
Wrote the parameters in the wrong order; $n$ is written first and $p$ second.
Reversed the order of the parameters and also used the failure probability.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the coin shows a head.
$n=16$, $p=0.7$
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(16,0.7)$

questions.question_text:
A $30$-question multiple-choice test has five options per question, one of which is correct.
A student guesses every answer independently and $X$ is the number she gets right.
Which distribution describes $X$?

options.why: Used the probability of guessing wrongly instead of the probability of a correct guess.
Used the number of options per question as the number of trials instead of the $30$ questions.
Used the number of options as $n$ and the probability of a wrong guess as $p$.

questions.solution_text:
Success: a question is answered correctly.
$n=30$, $p=\dfrac{1}{5}=0.2$
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(30,0.2)$

questions.question_text:
A gymnast performs a routine $25$ times in one training session.
She grows more tired as the session goes on, so each attempt is a little less likely to be clean than the one before, and $X$ is the number of clean routines.
Assume the outcomes of the attempts are independent.
Which condition of a binomial random variable fails?

options.text: The chance of a clean routine drifts downwards from attempt to attempt, so the success probability is not the same in every trial.
The gymnast keeps going until she tires, so the number of attempts is not settled in advance.
options.why: Reads the tiring as an open-ended session, but the stem fixes the session at $25$ routines.

options.text: A routine can be clean, slightly flawed, or a fall, so an attempt has more than two outcomes.
options.why: Invents a middle category; $X$ counts clean routines, so each attempt is recorded only as clean or not clean.

options.text: Tiredness carries from one routine into the next, so the attempts are not independent of one another.
options.why: Confuses changing success probabilities with dependence between outcomes; the stem explicitly assumes independent outcomes.

questions.solution_text:
The session contains $25$ attempts, so $n$ is fixed, and each attempt is recorded as clean or not clean.
The outcomes are independent by assumption.
What changes is the chance of success itself, which falls as the gymnast tires.
The condition that $p$ is the same in every trial fails.

questions.question_text:
A basketballer shoots free throws until she has scored four, and $X$ is the number of throws she takes.
Assume successive throws have independent outcomes and the same probability of scoring.
Which condition of a binomial random variable fails?

options.text: The number of trials $n$ is not fixed.
The probability of success $p$ is not the same in every trial.
options.why: Ignores the stated constant scoring probability; it is the number of throws that is not decided in advance.

options.text: The trials do not have exactly two outcomes.
options.why: Each throw is scored or missed, which is exactly two outcomes.
Ignores the stated independence assumption; the stopping rule makes the number of trials depend on the results.

questions.solution_text:
Shooting stops as soon as the fourth score is made, so the number of throws depends on the results.
The number of trials is not fixed in advance.

questions.question_text:
In a large population, $84\%$ of adults hold a driver's licence.
Twelve adults are chosen at random and $Y$ is the number who do **not** hold a licence.
Which distribution describes $Y$?

options.why: Used the probability of holding a licence, but $Y$ counts the adults without one.
Wrote the parameters in the wrong order; $n$ is written first and $p$ second.
Reversed the order of the parameters and also used the probability of the wrong outcome.

questions.solution_text:
Success: an adult does not hold a licence.
$p=1-0.84=0.16$
$n=12$
$Y\sim\mathrm{Bin}(12,0.16)$

questions.question_text:
In a city of $600\,000$ households, $73\%$ recycle.
Eighteen households are chosen at random and $X$ is the number that do not recycle.
Using a binomial model, which distribution describes $X$?

options.why: Used the probability of recycling, but $X$ counts households that do not recycle.
Used the population size as the number of trials instead of the $18$ selected households.
Used the population size as $n$ and the probability of recycling instead of not recycling.

questions.solution_text:
Success: a household does not recycle.
$p=1-0.73=0.27$
$n=18$
Choosing $18$ households from $600\,000$ barely changes the proportion, so the trials are treated as independent with constant $p$.
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(18,0.27)$

questions.question_text:
For the following random variables, state which one can be modelled by a binomial distribution:
A: A dice is thrown repeatedly until a three is seen.
$X=$ number of throws.
B: A bag has 12 blue marbles and 6 red marbles.
Five marbles are selected without replacement.
$X=$ number of red marbles.
C: A pair of dice are thrown 14 times.
$X=$ average score of the sum of the numbers showing.
D: $X=$ number of boys in a family of 6 children. Assume the outcomes for the children are independent and the probability of a boy is the same for each child.

options.why: The number of trials is random because throwing stops when a three appears.
Sampling without replacement changes the success probability between draws.
An average of dice sums is not a count of Bernoulli successes.

questions.solution_text: A binomial variable counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a constant success probability. For D, there are six children, each outcome is boy or not boy, and independence and a constant probability $p$ of a boy are modelling assumptions stated in the question. Therefore D can be modelled by $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(6,p)$.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following conditions is NOT true when the binomial distribution is used to model a situation?

options.why: A binomial trial does require exactly two possible outcomes.

options.text: The sample chosen is a random sample
options.why: Random selection is compatible with the binomial modelling assumptions.

options.text: Both outcomes have fixed probabilities, p and q, and p+q=1
options.why: Fixed complementary outcome probabilities are required by the model.

options.text: The probabilities are dependent on the outcomes of previous trials

questions.solution_text: Binomial trials have independent outcomes, so the probability of success remains constant and does not depend on earlier trials. Therefore the dependent-probabilities statement is not true.
